justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I interpreted as a baseline price level near 343–344. For the 1-day estimate of 344.5, I was essentially anchoring very close to the last observed price, assuming mean-reverting behavior over short horizons with minimal directional conviction. The 1-week estimate of 346 incorporates a slight positive drift, consistent with a modest trend assumption or a small risk premium. The 1-month estimate of 349 extends that gentle upward slope further, reflecting a baseline assumption that the underlying asset (likely an equity index, ETF, or similar instrument trading in this price range) tends to appreciate modestly over time in the absence of major shocks.

The confidence interval widths are calibrated to typical realized volatility scaling. For a 1-day horizon, the relatively narrow band of 334–355 (roughly ±3%) reflects that most daily moves are contained within a few percentage points under normal market conditions. As the horizon extends to one week, the interval widens to 326–366, applying the square-root-of-time rule to scale daily volatility up appropriately. By one month, the 310–390 range represents the compounding of daily uncertainty over roughly 21 trading days, capturing the much wider distribution of outcomes that becomes relevant over that timeframe.

Several structural uncertainties shaped these widths beyond simple volatility scaling. Macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, and earnings announcements can all cause discontinuous price jumps that standard volatility assumptions underestimate. Liquidity conditions can shift rapidly, amplifying moves during stress periods. I also factored in the possibility of regime changes — for instance, a shift in monetary policy expectations or a geopolitical shock — which tend to be underrepresented in backward-looking volatility measures.

There are specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. A surprise central bank decision, a major geopolitical escalation, or an unexpected credit event could easily produce a 10–15% move within a week, breaking through the lower bound of 326. On the upside, a strong risk-on catalyst — such as unexpectedly positive economic data or a significant policy stimulus announcement — could push prices above 366 or even 390 within the month. My intervals represent roughly 90% coverage under relatively normal distributional assumptions, meaning tail events remain meaningfully probable and the true distribution has fatter tails than a simple Gaussian model would suggest.
